This is JP Morgan’s view is Wall Street consensus. It assumes there is one Democratic Party. 

My view aligns more with Democrat Strategist Jim Carville, who spoke on the Bulwark podcast two weeks ago. He suggests there are two Democratic parties, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and the more moderate/traditional Democrats. These divisions mean the margin of victory might play a huge role in the market’s reaction.
--
Carville:
“I would be disappointed if it comes in at 225 House seats. That would almost be—I would rather the Republicans keep the House by five than the Democrats win by five because if that happens, they’re hostage to the DSA. Like, Hakeem [Jeffries] cannot move. He has nowhere to go. Even if you have a close Senate, [Sen. John] Fetterman would keep [Sen. Chuck] Schumer Pepto-Bismol all night. So I think this is one of those races where margin matters a lot.”
--

We would add that if the Senate is a 51-49 Democrat majority, not only does presumed Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer have to worry about PA Senator John Fetterman siding with Republicans, but Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and a presumed Michigan winner Abdul El-Sayed could put up a “block” because the Democratic Party is not progressive enough.

This issue would come to a head almost immediately over data centers.

Moderate/traditional Democrats, such as unions and middle-class voters, want those jobs. They are accelerationists. 

The DSA wants to block more data center construction. They are decelerationists.

This could turn into an epic fight within the Democratic Party.

article.plain_text:
National Institutes of Health (NIH) researchers demonstrated that tracking physical activity over a full year revealed almost twice as many disease risk factors as the one-week snapshots typically obtained by wearable studies.
Looking at health records and Fitbit data from nearly 30,000 participants in NIH’s All of UsResearch Program, the authors of the study drew associations between physical activity metrics, measured across timespans ranging from one day to one year, and disease outcomes up to 5 years later. In general, the researchers found that the longer measurement windows coincided with step-count being linked to a greater number of current and future diseases. The study associated one-year step count, for example, to nearly 120 more pre-existing diseases and 28 more future diseases than one-day step count did.
This study replicated many known associations but importantly unveiled new connections between step-count and conditions including autoimmune disorders and chronic pain syndrome.
The different pictures painted by short- and long-term data collection suggest that the standard one-week deployment of wearable devices may not fully reflect the effects of habitual behaviors. To get a better idea of what someone’s physical activity could tell us about their risk of disease, data from the NIH All of Us Research Program has shown that it could be necessary to take a much longer view.
Reference: Evelynne S. Fulda, et al. 11 million days of longitudinal Fitbit data reveal novel future health insights. Nature Communications. November 3, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78529-2
